newsitem.title: UK: Strong medicine not enough for Sears ills.
newsitem.headline: Strong medicine not enough for Sears ills.

text.p: Liam Strong, beleaguered chief executive of Sears Plc, put his reputation on the line when he took on the job of revitalising the rambling British retail empire back in 1992.
Everyone agreed it was a mammoth task, but even he probably did not realise how tough it would be to streamline such a sprawling business and get it firing on all cylinders.
Strong, now 52, moved to Sears after making his name as a marketing high flier at the newly privatised British Airways.
There were high hopes his skills could help make sense of Sears's rag bag of businesses, which ranged from London's Selfridges department store to housebuilding and jewellery.
A military historian, with American Civil War general Ulysses S. Grant as one of his heroes, Strong began a campaign which radically changed the look of the company.

Menswear retailing, shoe manufacturing, housebuilding, property investment, Dutch mail order, Olympus sports and now Freemans mail order, have all gone. Freemans, the latest disposal, is being sold to Littlewoods, the second biggest player in the British mail order market.

But retail analysts say the pruning has not been tough enough. Sears' shares, now 88 pence each, are still underperforming and last week the company had to warn investors that profits this year would be lower than last year's 100.1 million pounds ($168 million).

Shareholders are pressing for Sears to ditch its shoe division completely. Some want to demerge Selfridges, to unlock the value of the group's most profitable business. Sears is promising a 410 million pound cash payout following the sale of Freemans, but this alone may not satisfy disaffected investors.

Pressure on Strong has intensified as shareholders have become increasingly impatient with his failure to deliver the promised recovery. "Strong must go, say Sears' investors" ran the headline in the latest edition of the Sunday Times.
But with the backing of his chairman Sir Bob Reid and with no obvious successor, Strong looks set to battle on for the foreseeable future.
Born in Enniskillen, Northern Ireland, Strong was educated at Portora Royal School and Trinity College, Dublin, where he took an honours degree in philosophy and psychology.

He started his business career with U.S. consumer products giant Procter and Gamble, moving to Reckitt & Colman in 1975. In 1989 he switched to British Airways, where he was director of marketing and operations.
He joined the Sears board in November 1991 and became chief executive on February 14, 1992.
Married with two children his hobbies include walking, sailing, shooting and opera. ($1=.5974 Pound)
